chapter_theme: Youth does not last: old age, the loss of friends and the decay of the beloved's body come to everyone, and death can take the young as well as the old. The wise therefore renounce early and do virtue while they have the means.
structure_note: Quatrains 11-18 picture the coming of old age, several through the desired woman who will herself grow old (14, 17); 19-20 turn to death's taking the young, and urge virtue without delay.

11.reading: Knowing that grey hair will come, the wise renounced in childhood itself, while those who delighted in faulty, fleeting youth will later rise painfully leaning on a staff.
11.nuance: குழவியிடத்தே ('in infancy') pushes renunciation as early as language allows; the verse treats the foresight of age, not age itself, as the mark of wisdom.

12.reading: The cords of friendship are cut, those once close have drawn back, the bonds of love have come loose: look within and ask what profit there is in living on, for misery has come as on a sinking ship.
12.nuance: The verse is spoken to an ageing person, perhaps the speaker himself (உட்காணாய், 'look within'). Pope's 'joyous life' is his addition; the Tamil asks only about the gain of living.

positions.position: நல்லார் are women, whose affection has waned.
நல்லார் are the learned and good, who have lessened their closeness.

13.reading: Those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff, walk unsteadily and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire until the body is scorned, have no way to the path of safety.
13.nuance: Both commentators take the 'path of safety' as the way to release and இல்செறிந்து as clinging to household life, so the verse faults not old age but desire that outlives the body's capacity.

14.reading: When a once-desired woman, bent, frail, head shaking and leaning on a staff, comes to hold the staff her mother held, she becomes a torment to men of unsteady mind who still desire her.
14.nuance: அணங்கு is read by Mudaliar as an enchanting goddess and by Shanmuganar and Pope as pain; the line is hard, and the readings below differ on whose mother is meant.

positions.position: அம்மனைக்கோல் is the staff of her own mother.
Her staff looks to the men like the staff their own mother leaned on, and that pains them.

15.reading: My mother left me here and went in search of her mother, and that mother did the same; this world goes on, mother seeking mother, a pitiable thing.
15.nuance: Shanmuganar reads the 'seeking' as taking a new birth, so the chain is the cycle of births; Pope and Mudaliar keep it as each generation following the last into death. அளித்து is read as 'pitiable' by Mudaliar's gloss எளிமையுடைத்து; Pope renders it ironically as 'grace'.

16.reading: The fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the tender leaves of the garland held before it in the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise.
16.nuance: The garland that feeds the lamb is the sign of its slaughter: youthful pleasure is enjoyed in the presence of what ends it.

17.reading: Youth falls as fruit drops from every tree in a cool grove; do not desire this woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
17.nuance: The wordplay turns வேல்கண்ணள் (spear-eyed) into கோல்கண்ணள் (staff-eyed): the same compound form names her beauty and her decline.

18.reading: Because others ask in turn, 'How old are you? How are your teeth? Do you still eat twice?', and so examine one's body, the wise do not count on the body's vigour.
18.nuance: The questions are polite and routine; the verse's point is that such solicitude already treats one as declining. Mudaliar records two readings of இருசிகை, a second mouthful or two meals a day.

19.reading: Do not say 'we are young, we will learn good deeds later'; while wealth is in hand, do virtue without hiding it, for a harsh wind can drop good unripe fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
19.nuance: Mudaliar notes the alternative reading of கனி ஒழிய as 'the ripe fruit remaining on the tree', which sharpens the point: death may take the young and leave the old.

20.reading: Since merciless Death roams looking for his people, take provisions for the journey in good time; it is well to keep his stealth in mind, for he takes even the unborn child while its mother wails.
20.nuance: Mudaliar reads தோட்கோப்பு, a bundle carried on the shoulder, as the good deeds one needs for the next world; Pope renders it 'wallet'. The verse leaves the provisions as a figure.

positions.position: The shoulder-bundle is the stock of good deeds needed for the next world.

links.note: Here the wise renounce the world even in childhood. Kural 46 asks what a person living household life by virtue would gain by going the outer way. The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Parimelazhagar and Pope do, and துறந்தார் here as world-renunciation, as Shanmuganar does.
Kural 342 says renounce while there is time; this quatrain pushes the right time back to infancy, because age is certain.
Both take the spear-like eye of conventional praise and undo it: 17 by age, which makes it a staff-guided eye, 44 by anatomy, which makes it a scooped-out palm fruit.
Both quote the procrastinator's words, 'we will know it later' (மற்றறிவாம் here, அன்றறிவாம் in the Kural), and reject them. The Naladiyar's reason is that the young die too.

new_concepts.gloss: youth, as a stage that passes
new_concepts.label_source: The chapter title இளமை நிலையாமை and quatrain 11 use the word.

new_concepts.gloss: the body, as a perishable and impure frame
new_concepts.label_source: The verses use யாக்கை (18, 27, 28, 30, 34) and the chapter title யாக்கை நிலையாமை.

source_issues: Quatrain 16: Mudaliar's commentary begins with glosses on this quatrain and then continues with the closing of his note on quatrain 7 (the citation of Kural 37 and the sun-as-measure figure). Only the opening glosses belong here.
Quatrain 20: Shanmuganar's commentary is missing; the field holds only the heading of the next chapter.
Quatrain 14: Mudaliar glosses சென்றாள், a word not in the printed quatrain, which suggests a variant text.
